summary: For 11–12 year-olds: energy loss between trophic levels. The core idea is that only roughly 10% (a teaching rule of thumb) of the energy at one level passes to the next; the rest is transferred OUT of the chain — as heat from respiration, energy used in movement, and energy in undigested waste and uneaten parts — not destroyed. Pupils should derive, not merely state, that this is WHY energy pyramids are always wide at the base and narrow at the top (and biomass pyramids usually are), WHY food chains rarely exceed four or five links, and why eating lower on a chain feeds more people. Note that pyramids of numbers can be inverted (e.g. one oak tree supporting many caterpillars), because they count individuals rather than energy or mass. Anchor everything in the compounding worked chain 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 kJ.
misconceptions: Thinking energy is 'used up' or destroyed rather than transferred out of the chain as heat/waste (violating conservation of energy).
Believing energy is passed on efficiently, so it's puzzling why chains are short or pyramids narrow.
Confusing energy flow (one-way, lost each step) with matter/nutrient cycling (recycled) — assuming energy also cycles.
Assuming top predators have the most energy because they are biggest/strongest, rather than the least available energy.

activities.title: Watch the energy leak up the pyramid
steps: Start with a fixed pot of energy (e.g. 10,000 kJ) at the producer level at the wide base.

Move up one level and track what reaches it: roughly 10% passes on while about 90% peels off along labelled streams — heat from respiration, energy burned in movement, energy locked in waste and uneaten parts.
Follow the running total up the levels: 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 kJ, saying the proportion lost each step aloud.
Try to add a fifth or sixth level and notice there is essentially no energy left to support it; state in your own words why food chains are short.
Change the transfer efficiency between 5%, 10% and 20% and describe how the pyramid steepens or flattens and how many levels become possible.
activities.insight: Because only about a tenth of the energy survives each transfer, far less energy — and therefore usually far less living mass — is available at each higher level, which gives the energy pyramid its wide-base/narrow-top shape, makes most biomass pyramids the same shape, and limits chain length. 'Lost' means transferred out as heat/movement/waste, obeying conservation of energy.

activities.title: Lift-the-flap pyramid for pre-teaching and reference
steps: Tap or lift each level of a labelled energy pyramid to reveal its loss breakdown: '~90% lost as heat (respiration), movement, waste; ~10% passed on'.
Read off the fixed worked example 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 kJ and restate where each lost portion goes.
Name the shape (wide base, narrow top) and explain in one sentence how it follows from the 10% rule.
activities.insight: The ~10% rule and the named loss pathways crisply introduce or revise the concept and connect the pyramid shape to the rule.

activities.title: Reason it out loud: why can't the chain be longer?
steps: Answer the prompt: 'Only about 10% of the energy at one level reaches the next. When a rabbit eats grass, what happens to the other ~90% of the grass's energy — is it destroyed?'
Name at least two places the missing energy actually goes (heat from respiration, movement, undigested waste).
Explain why a field can feed many rabbits but only a few foxes, using the energy available rather than animal size or strength.
Explain why food chains almost never have more than about five links.
activities.insight: Verbalising where the energy goes and tying predator scarcity to the energy budget distinguishes genuine energy-tracking reasoning from rote recall.

activities.title: Check the quantitative reasoning
steps: Given a producer level of 10,000 kJ, calculate how much energy reaches the fourth trophic level by applying ~10% three times (fill-in-the-blank proportional chain: 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 kJ).
Choose and justify why food chains are short in energy terms, rather than just naming the rule.
Put the loss pathways (heat/respiration, movement, waste, uneaten) in the right place at a transfer.
Decide whether you would expect a greater mass of foxes than of rabbits in the same field, and explain in energy terms why this is very unlikely.
activities.insight: The learner can apply the ~10% rule quantitatively and explain pyramid shape and chain-length limits, transferring the reasoning to the biomass question.

checkQuestion: Say: 'Only about 10% of the energy at one level reaches the next. When a rabbit eats grass, what happens to the other roughly 90% of the grass's energy — is it destroyed? Then use your answer to explain why a field can feed lots of rabbits but only a few foxes.'
checkAnswer: The energy is NOT destroyed — it is transferred out of the food chain, mostly as heat released during respiration, plus energy used for movement and energy lost in undigested waste (droppings). Because only about 10% passes up at each level, far less energy is available higher up, so the same field can support only a few foxes but many rabbits.
